opus-5.5.text:
I think there are two kinds of joy in research, and they come at different stages.

In the early stage, when a field is wide open, the excitement is in exploration. Nobody knows which direction is right, so you try many ideas. A lot of them fail, but every so often something surprising works, and you get that feeling of discovering something new about the world. When I started working on generative models, GANs and image synthesis were exactly like that. Every few months someone found a new trick, a new architecture, and the quality jumped. It felt like walking in a dark room and occasionally finding a light switch.

As a field matures, the nature of the work changes. Once the community converges on a few promising recipes, like large-scale training of diffusion or autoregressive models, the question is less "what might work?" and more "how do we make this actually work at scale, reliably, for real problems?" That's more like engineering a building than wandering through a forest. Some people find that less romantic, but I find it deeply satisfying in a different way. You set an ambitious goal, say a world model that can simulate physical environments well enough to train robots or autonomous vehicles, and you have to organize data, compute, infrastructure and a team to get there. When it finally comes together and people start using it, the impact is much bigger than a single clever paper.

I also don't think the two stages are fully separate. Even when executing, you hit problems no one has solved, and you have to go back into exploration mode for a while. The skill is knowing when to keep exploring and when to commit. Committing too early means you might bet on the wrong thing; exploring too long means the field moves past you.

So for me the appeal has shifted from the thrill of discovery toward the thrill of building something real. Both are valuable, and I think good researchers today need to be comfortable moving between the two.

r002.rationale: The response values team-based execution while describing renewed exploration when execution reveals unsolved problems, and says researchers need to move between the two.

fable-5.1.text:
It's a question I think about a lot, because I've lived through both phases. When I started in this field, research felt like wandering through a huge dark room with a small flashlight. You'd pick a direction almost on instinct, and most of the time you'd hit a wall. But every once in a while you'd find a door nobody knew was there, and that feeling was addictive. The appeal was the exploration itself.

Now the room is much brighter. We know, roughly, where the doors are. Scaling works, data quality matters, the recipes are more or less understood. So the question becomes less "what is possible" and more "who can actually build it, at what cost, how fast, and how well." For some people that feels like a loss. The romance of discovery is replaced by engineering, infrastructure, iteration. I understand that feeling.

But I honestly don't see it as less appealing. I see it as a different kind of appeal. There is enormous creativity in execution. Getting a video model or a world model to actually work at scale is not just turning a crank. You still hit problems nobody has solved, they're just hiding inside the details: how you curate data, how you design the training curriculum, how you make something that runs in real time instead of in a paper. Every one of those is a research problem, it's just that the result now has to survive contact with reality.

And there's something deeply satisfying about that. Earlier in my career, I'd publish a paper and maybe a few hundred people would read it. Now when something works, it ends up in the hands of millions of people, or it becomes the foundation that robots or simulations are built on. The feedback loop is shorter and much more honest. Reality is a tougher reviewer than any conference.

I'd also say the exploration hasn't gone away, it's just moved. The frontier shifts. Ten years ago the frontier was "can we generate a plausible image at all." Today it's physical AI, world models, agents that reason about space and time, systems that understand cause and effect. Those are wide open. So I tell young researchers: don't be nostalgic for an era you think was more adventurous. The adventure is still here, you just have to go a bit further to find it, and you have to be willing to build things to get there.

astra-6.text:
I think the appeal changes, but it doesn’t disappear. When you’re exploring, the excitement comes from possibility: Can we make this work? Is there a different way to approach the problem? As you move toward building a solution, the excitement becomes seeing an idea actually work and become useful.

And execution brings its own research questions. Something may work in a small experiment, but making it reliable exposes limitations you didn’t understand before. That can send you back to explore new ideas. So I don’t see exploration and execution as completely separate phases. The interaction between them is a big part of what makes AI research interesting.

r002.rationale: It describes exploration and execution as interacting, but does not advocate disciplined team execution alongside major innovation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the appeal changes, but it doesn’t disappear. When you’re exploring, the excitement comes from asking, “What might be possible?” As you start building, the question becomes, “Can we actually make this work?” That brings a different kind of creativity. You have to choose what matters, understand why something fails, and keep improving it.

For me, those two stages feed each other. Building a solution often exposes something you don’t understand, and that becomes the next research question. So I don’t see execution as the end of exploration. It’s another way to discover what’s worth exploring.

r002.rationale: It describes execution and exploration as mutually reinforcing, but does not advocate disciplined team execution combined with major innovation where opportunities remain.
